prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Lessons learned from previous successful airliner ditchings helped pilot C.B. "Sully" Sullenberger save 155 lives when he put his US Airways A320 jetliner down in the Hudson River, a fellow pilot told CNN. An Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 is seen just before it crashes into the sea off the Comoro Islands in 1996. Twenty-three people died when an Overseas National Airways DC-9 ditched off the Caribbean island of St. Croix in 1970, and 123 were killed in the crash of an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 off the Comoro Islands near Africa in 1996. But Emilio Corsetti, an Airbus 320 pilot and aviation author, said those ditchings were actually successful "because people were able to get out" -- 40 in the 1970 crash and 52 in the 1996 incident. More may have survived if those planes were equipped like the Airbus 320 and if passengers followed standard evacuation procedures, Corsetti told CNN.  Watch how to survive a plane crash » . In fact, Corsetti said, the 1970 crash helped lead to a redesign of seat belts. The belts aboard the DC-9 were "metal-to-fabric," Corsetti said, depending upon tension to keep passengers strapped in their seats. "Those things gave out... People were thrown out of their seats 10 rows up," said Corsetti, who has written a book, "35 Miles from Shore," about the 1970 crash. On the Hudson River on Thursday, the impact was like "being inside a car that crashes," passenger Alberto Panero said. Corsetti also said that the DC-9 didn't have life raft capacity for all those aboard. Unlike the A320's escape slides, which helped dozens of passengers get out, the DC-9s rafts could hold only three or four. In the 1996 crash, the Ethiopian Airlines 767 was attempting a water landing off the Grand Comoro Island during a hijacking. The plane had run out of fuel. While it is uncertain whether there was a struggle in the cockpit, video shows the 767 nearing the ocean's surface. As it does, the plane's left engine hits a reef, Corsetti said, sending it into a cartwheel. He said the majority of the 123 who died drowned. They had put on life vests and inflated them before they could get out of the splintered fuselage, he said, and were trapped against the bulkheads as water filled the wreckage. Sullenberger had other advantages, too, Corsetti said. Putting the jetliner down into the placid Hudson River probably helped him keep the plane level. The DC-9 pilot faced 8- to 15-foot seas in the 1970 ditching and the Ethiopian jet was dealing with offshore waves.  Watch a pilot describe how plane went down » . The A320 also is equipped with a ditching button, Corsetti said, which closes all valves below the waterline, enabling it to float more easily. No matter the lessons learned from the earlier crashes, US Airways passengers were happy Sullenberger was in the cockpit Thursday. "He's the man! He's absolutely the man!" passenger Vince Spera said. "If you want to talk to a hero, get a hold of him because that is the hero in this whole deal." CNN's Wayne Drash contributed to this report.

**(CNN) —** Lessons learned from previous successful airliner ditchings helped pilot C.B. “Sully” Sullenberger save 155 lives when he brought his US Airways Airbus A320 down on the Hudson River, a fellow pilot told CNN.

An Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 is seen moments before crashing into the sea off the Comoro Islands in 1996.

Twenty-three people died when an Overseas National Airways DC-9 ditched off the Caribbean island of St. Croix in 1970, while 123 were killed when an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 crashed off the Comoro Islands near Africa in 1996.

However, Emilio Corsetti, an Airbus A320 pilot and aviation author, said those ditchings were, in fact, successful “because people were able to get out”—40 in the 1970 crash and 52 in the 1996 incident.

More people might have survived had those aircraft been equipped like the Airbus A320 and had passengers followed standard evacuation procedures, Corsetti told CNN.

**Watch how to survive a plane crash »**

Corsetti said the 1970 crash helped prompt a redesign of seat belts. The belts aboard the DC-9 used a “metal-to-fabric” design that relied on tension to keep passengers secured in their seats.

“Those things gave out.... People were thrown out of their seats 10 rows up,” said Corsetti, who wrote *35 Miles from Shore*, a book about the 1970 crash.

During Thursday’s landing on the Hudson River, the impact felt like “being inside a car that crashes,” passenger Alberto Panero said.

Corsetti also noted that the DC-9 lacked sufficient life-raft capacity for everyone aboard. Unlike the A320’s escape slides, which helped dozens of passengers evacuate, the DC-9’s rafts could hold only three or four people.

In the 1996 crash, the Ethiopian Airlines 767 was attempting a water landing off Grand Comoro Island during a hijacking after running out of fuel. Although it remains unclear whether there was a struggle in the cockpit, video footage shows the 767 approaching the ocean’s surface. As it did so, the plane’s left engine struck a reef, Corsetti said, sending the aircraft into a cartwheel.

He said that most of the 123 people who died drowned. They had put on their life vests and inflated them before escaping the splintered fuselage, leaving them trapped against the bulkheads as water filled the wreckage.

Sullenberger had other advantages as well, Corsetti said. Bringing the jetliner down on the placid Hudson River probably helped him keep the aircraft level. By contrast, the DC-9 pilot encountered seas of 8 to 15 feet during the 1970 ditching, while the Ethiopian jet faced offshore waves.

**Watch a pilot describe how the plane went down »**

The A320 is also equipped with a ditching button, Corsetti said. The button closes all valves below the waterline, allowing the aircraft to float more easily.

Regardless of the lessons learned from the earlier crashes, US Airways passengers were grateful that Sullenberger was in the cockpit Thursday.

“He’s the man! He’s absolutely the man!” passenger Vince Spera said. “If you want to talk to a hero, get a hold of him because that is the hero in this whole deal.”

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — According to fellow pilot and aviation writer Emilio Corsetti, knowledge gained from earlier airliner water landings helped Capt. C.B. “Sully” Sullenberger rescue 155 people when he landed a US Airways Airbus A320 on New York’s Hudson River.

Previous ditchings had far higher death tolls. In 1970, an Overseas National Airways DC-9 came down in the sea near the Caribbean island of St. Croix, killing 23 people. In 1996, an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 crashed into the ocean near Africa’s Comoro Islands, leaving 123 dead. Images captured the Ethiopian jet shortly before it struck the water.

Corsetti, who flies the Airbus A320, nevertheless described both incidents as successful ditchings because some occupants escaped. Forty people survived the 1970 accident, while 52 got out alive in 1996. He told CNN that the survival totals might have been higher had the aircraft offered equipment comparable to the A320’s and had passengers observed normal evacuation rules.

Watch advice on surviving an aircraft accident »

Corsetti said the St. Croix crash contributed to changes in seat-belt design. The DC-9 used “metal-to-fabric” restraints that relied on tension to hold occupants in place. Those belts failed, he said, causing some passengers to be hurled as far as 10 rows forward. Corsetti wrote about that accident in his book, “35 Miles from Shore.”

Describing Thursday’s impact on the Hudson, passenger Alberto Panero compared the experience to being inside a car during a collision.

The DC-9 also lacked enough life-raft space for everyone aboard, Corsetti noted. Its rafts could carry only three or four people, unlike the A320’s evacuation slides, which enabled dozens of passengers to leave the aircraft.

The 1996 Ethiopian Airlines crash occurred as the fuel-starved 767 tried to land on the water near Grand Comoro Island during a hijacking. It remains unclear whether a confrontation was taking place in the cockpit. Video footage shows the aircraft approaching the sea before its left engine struck a reef, Corsetti said, causing the jet to cartwheel.

Most of the 123 victims drowned, according to Corsetti. They had already put on and inflated their life jackets before escaping the shattered fuselage. As water entered the wreckage, the inflated vests pinned them against interior bulkheads.

Corsetti said Sullenberger also benefited from more favorable conditions. The calm Hudson River likely made it easier to keep the A320 level. By contrast, the DC-9 pilot confronted seas of 8 to 15 feet in 1970, while the Ethiopian crew had to contend with waves offshore.

Watch a pilot explain how the aircraft came down »

Another advantage was the A320’s ditching control, Corsetti said. Activating it shuts valves located below the waterline, helping the aircraft remain afloat.

Whatever role earlier accidents played in improving safety, the US Airways passengers were grateful that Sullenberger was flying on Thursday.

“He’s the man! He’s absolutely the man!” passenger Vince Spera said. “If you want to talk to a hero, get a hold of him because that is the hero in this whole deal.”

CNN’s Wayne Drash contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
Pilot C.B. “Sully” Sullenberger’s successful landing of a US Airways Airbus A320 on the Hudson River drew on lessons learned from earlier airliner ditchings. Those previous accidents demonstrated how aircraft design, emergency equipment, crew preparation, and the conditions of a water landing could determine whether passengers survived. When Sullenberger ditched the A320 in January 2009, all 155 people aboard were rescued.

Two earlier incidents were especially instructive. In 1970, a DC-9 was forced to ditch, and in 1996 an Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 attempted a water landing after being hijacked and running out of fuel. Both accidents caused many deaths, but they were still regarded as partly successful ditchings because 40 people escaped from the DC-9 and 52 survived the Ethiopian Airlines crash.

The 1970 accident revealed important weaknesses in cabin safety systems. Some tension-based seat belts failed during impact, allowing passengers to be thrown from their seats. The findings contributed to the development of more reliable seat-belt designs. The evacuation also exposed the consequences of inadequate flotation equipment: limited life-raft capacity made it harder for survivors to remain safe after leaving the aircraft.

By contrast, the A320’s evacuation equipment played a major role in the Hudson River rescue. Its escape slides could also function as flotation devices, helping dozens of passengers leave the aircraft and stay out of the freezing water while rescue boats approached.

The Ethiopian Airlines accident illustrated another danger associated with ditching near a coastline. As the fuel-starved 767 descended toward the ocean, its left engine struck a reef close to the surface. The impact caused the aircraft to break apart, turning an already difficult emergency landing into a catastrophic crash. Together, these earlier events provided valuable lessons that helped improve aircraft restraints, evacuation systems, crew procedures, and the overall understanding of how to survive a water landing.
outputs.L4:
Long before US Airways Flight 1549 landed on the Hudson River, investigators had studied other airliner ditchings to understand why some occupants survived while others did not. Those accidents revealed that survival depended on more than the pilot’s ability to place an aircraft on the water. Cabin design, restraint systems, emergency equipment, crew training, passenger behavior, and the speed of rescue all played critical roles.

Earlier ditchings showed that the impact itself was often only the first danger. Poorly secured passengers could suffer serious injuries, while damaged exits, flooding cabins, and confusion could delay evacuation. Investigations led to stronger seats and improved seat belts, clearer emergency instructions, better-marked exits, and more reliable emergency lighting. Aircraft were also equipped with escape slides capable of carrying large numbers of people and, on some routes, serving as flotation devices. Life vests and other survival equipment became easier to locate and use.

Evacuation procedures also evolved. Flight attendants were trained to assess conditions outside each exit, prevent passengers from opening doors where water or hazards made escape unsafe, and redirect them toward usable exits. Repeated commands, rapid movement, and leaving baggage behind became central parts of emergency training. Past accidents had demonstrated that even a survivable landing could become deadly if passengers hesitated, blocked aisles, inflated life vests inside the cabin, or attempted to take possessions with them.

These accumulated lessons helped shape the response when Flight 1549 struck a flock of Canada geese shortly after departing New York’s LaGuardia Airport on January 15, 2009. With both engines losing thrust and little altitude available, Captain C.B. “Sully” Sullenberger and First Officer Jeffrey Skiles determined that the Airbus A320 could not safely reach a nearby airport. Sullenberger instead guided the aircraft into the Hudson River, keeping it largely level and intact during the impact.

The cabin crew immediately ordered an evacuation. Passengers used the forward exits and overwing exits, gathering on the wings and on deployed escape slides as water entered the aircraft. Seat belts had helped protect occupants during the landing, while the aircraft’s exits, slides, flotation equipment, and established evacuation procedures enabled people to leave quickly. Nearby ferries and emergency boats reached the scene within minutes, limiting the danger from freezing water and winter temperatures.

All 155 passengers and crew members survived. The outcome resulted from exceptional flying and crew coordination, but it also reflected decades of lessons learned from earlier emergencies. Each previous accident had exposed weaknesses and prompted changes in aircraft construction, restraint systems, safety equipment, training, and evacuation rules. The Hudson River landing demonstrated how those reforms, combined with disciplined action and a rapid rescue response, could turn a catastrophic engine failure into one of aviation’s most remarkable survival stories.
outputs.L5:
## Lessons from Sully: Courage, Preparation, and Leadership

CNN’s coverage of Captain Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger introduced millions of people to the extraordinary story of US Airways Flight 1549. On January 15, 2009, the aircraft struck a flock of birds shortly after takeoff, disabling both engines. Sully made the difficult decision to land the plane on New York’s Hudson River. All 155 people on board survived.

The event offers several important lessons. First, preparation matters. Sully’s successful landing was not simply the result of instinct or luck; it reflected decades of training and experience. In a crisis, people often depend on habits and knowledge developed long before the emergency begins.

Second, effective leadership requires calm decision-making. With only a few minutes to act, Sully assessed the available options, communicated clearly with his crew, and accepted responsibility for his choice. His composure helped others remain focused during an extremely dangerous situation.

Another lesson is the value of teamwork. Although Sully became the public face of the “Miracle on the Hudson,” the safe outcome also depended on the flight crew, air traffic controllers, rescue teams, ferry operators, and first responders. CNN interviews and reports highlighted how many individuals contributed to saving the passengers.

Finally, Sully’s story demonstrates that leadership can be questioned even after success. Investigators carefully examined whether the plane could have returned to an airport. This scrutiny showed the difference between computer simulations and real-world decisions made under pressure.

Sully’s actions remain a powerful example of professionalism, humility, and courage. The lasting lesson is simple: heroes are often people who prepare thoroughly, work with others, and remain calm when circumstances demand their best.

Sorry, I can’t reproduce that news story verbatim, but I can summarize it:

All 155 people aboard US Airways Flight 1549 survived the Hudson River ditching because of a combination of skilled piloting, favorable conditions, aircraft design, and improved safety equipment. Modern seat belts and strengthened cabin features helped passengers withstand the impact. Flight attendants quickly directed the evacuation, using inflatable slides—some serving as rafts—while passengers’ life vests provided added protection, despite some confusion over how and when to inflate them.

The river was relatively calm, allowing the Airbus A320 to remain afloat long enough for nearby ferries and emergency crews to rescue everyone. The aircraft’s “ditching” button also helped by closing external valves and openings below the waterline, slowing the entry of water. Together, these factors turned a potentially catastrophic water landing into a rare aviation disaster with no fatalities.
